newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Swiss gold traders weigh London against Zurich.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Swiss gold traders weigh London against Zurich.

text.p: Swiss banks, traditionally big players in the world gold market, are pondering a shift of certain activities to London as a result of changes in the precious metals business in recent years.

"I think we have a trend towards a two-tier market, with trade in physical gold centred in Zurich and trade in new products and derivatives from London," said one senior executive of a leading Swiss bank.
Many bankers see London as the acknowledged European centre for the derivatives business but Switzerland plays a key role in physical trade.
About one-third of the world's gold trade passes through Switzerland and big banks have their own refineries here.

The split in the gold business has become more apparent in the past decade because of strong growth in trade in derivatives instruments, a key element for risk management. Instruments include gold futures traded in New York and Tokyo and over-the-counter options traded heavily in London.
Swiss banks are reluctant to discuss their gold strategy in depth in public. "It is a famously discreet business," one London-based analyst said.

But among the big three -- Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), Credit Suisse, and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) -- there is some discussion about whether derivatives and forward trade, for example, ought to be run more from London.
One banker said his bank would keep some gold activities in Switzerland and had no plans to drop any of its business.
"We will continue to uphold our presence here, our strategy is to be a full-service provider," he said.
But he did not rule out changes which would create synergies by concentrating some activities in either centre.
"We traded OTC options from London for a long time, and we are now examining the strategy to determine if this strategy would also be appropriate for forward business," he said.
At Union Bank of Switzerland, Martyn Konig, deputy global head of commodities trading, denied market talk that the bank had moved its Zurich-based gold activities to London.
"We are actively trading in Zurich and London markets," he said. But he did not rule out some changes in future.

The bank has centralised its precious metals risk management and trading activities in Switzerland and was considering whether it would move some activities to London, where it also is a market-maker in gold bullion.
Any plans have not been finalised.
At SBC Warburg, Ed Mount, managing director and global head of metals, said Switzerland would continue to play a key role in gold trade in part because of its safe-haven status.
"Switzerland will remain a safe haven for the global community to store assets including physical gold," Mount said.
He said SBC was firmly involved in physical gold trade. He declined to elaborate on what, if any changes were being considered for any trading activities.
"Global technology advances make risk management services less geographically dependent," he said.

Physical gold trade involving gold bars, bullion and coins, is still heavily concentrated in Switzerland. Switzerland imports between 1,200 and 1,400 tonnes of the precious metal annually and exports about 90 percent of that, bankers said.

Historically, Switzerland has been a major centre for physical gold trade. Its position was reinforced after Swiss banks leaped into the breach in March 1968 when the London gold market closed for several days.
Swiss banks formed a "pool" to handle the output of the largest single producer, South Africa. They also handled much of the output of the former Soviet Union in the 1970s.
However, analysts note producers in North America and Australia have gained market share, and these depend on non-European centres to market gold.
Gold, the classic hedge against inflation, has also lost lustre as private investors switch to other assets.

"Switzerland in general was a much bigger centre for physical investment in gold 15 years ago. They (the Swiss bnaks) were worldwide distributors and had a homegrown market for investors. Now the market is much more based on derivatives," one London-based expert said.
Zurich has also seen the number of market participants decrease over time because of bank mergers and consolidations.
"The number of players has decreased. Ten years ago we had several banks, including the cantonal banks, and private banks, as active market makers," one Swiss banker said.
Credit Suisse Group, for example, as part of a restructuring, is centralising gold trade at Credit Suisse First Boston.

As a result, gold trade will cease at one of its subsidiaries, Bank Leu, at the end of March. It already closed gold trade at another subsidiary, former Swiss Volksbank, which took over Credit Suisse's domestic banking activities.
Some analysts believe that ultimately, Switzerland and London will enhance each other's business.
"I think it would be wrong to think that the Swiss banks are moving camp to London," said Tony Warwick-Ching, consultant at CRU International.
Warwick-Ching expected the Swiss banks would likely keep their core business in Switzerland, without excluding some shifts in other types of business.
"London has thrived on the more innovative business. What we are looking at is a position in which the two centres complement each other," he said.
